skillnav.method:
Section 4 separates data construction, expert training and routing. The authors synthesize 450 instruction/trajectory pairs for each of five skills: direction, vertical movement, stopping, landmarks and regions. They additionally synthesize 2,000 temporal-order examples. Paths have 4–7 steps and are filtered by skill-specific rules; GPT-4o supplies captions. A DUET backbone first learns from R2R plus ScaleVLN (or SRDF) and temporal data. Five copies are then specialized on the corresponding 450-example sets. Temporal reasoning is therefore a training and routing operation, not a sixth execution expert.

At inference, a frozen language model rewrites the instruction into execution order (Eq.2). A visual-language router uses the instruction, observed history and previous subgoals to infer the current subgoal and choose one expert (Eqs 3–5). The selected expert receives the ORIGINAL instruction, current observations and DUET map (Eq 6). This distinction matters for a rewriting control: changing the executor's instruction would test a different intervention. ScaleVLN uses CLIP-B/16 and BERT features; the SRDF variant uses InternViT-6B features.

Expert learning inherits supervised DUET behavior cloning/DAgger. In the inspected training path, each valid step contributes −log πθ(a*_t|I,O_t,M_t), summed over non-padding targets and scaled by the imitation weight and batch size. I is instruction text, O_t the visual observation, M_t the map, and a*_t an expert action over the current candidate set plus STOP. The frozen router has no gradient update. Five stored experts and the routing model still incur memory/API cost, even though only one expert executes at each step. Appendix F and released scripts disagree on some batch-size/learning-rate values, as recorded below.
skillnav.results:
Table 2 reports ScaleVLN-based R2R val-unseen SR/SPL rising from approximately 79/70 to 83/77, while the stronger SRDF baseline remains near 84/78. This makes backbone strength and training data essential controls. Appendix G/Table 13 provides the most important attribution check: Temporal DUET alone reaches 82.59 SR/75.40 SPL, while full SkillNav reaches 82.59/76.50. Most R2R improvement is already present before specialist routing.

Other settings show useful gains: GSA-N-Scene SPL rises roughly 43→48 for ScaleVLN and 43→45 for SRDF. Zero-shot RxR SR rises 26.8→30.3 and 21.4→31.8, respectively. Random routing gives 43.17 GSA-N-Scene SPL versus 47.96 for the Qwen router; instruction reordering adds 2.53 SPL. However, the mixed-skill agent outperforms the landmark specialist in Table 5 (48.90 versus 31.53 SR), so specialization is not uniformly beneficial. Appendix I.3's17-case analysis finds the landmark specialist optimal in 13 failures but selected correctly only once. These support grounded routing as a remaining problem, not a claim that routing is already solved.

mapnav.method: Construct M∈R^((n+4)×W×H): obstacle, explored, current-position, trajectory channels plus n semantic classes. Mask2Former segments RGB , depth gives point cloud, pose aligns successive observations, and projection updates BEV. Connected components over each semantic category above areaτ get centroid text labels, making a rendered ASM. Shared SigLIP-so400m encodes current RGB and ASM; spatial unpadding/patch merge Φ_spatial produces visual patches, separate 2 layer GELU projectors map to Qwen 2-7 B hidden space (Eqs 1–3). LLaVA-OneVision generates text commands; regex Ψ(text, patterns) maps synonyms to Forward/Left/Right/Stop (Eq 4). No differentiability through mapping/regex is claimed by its 'end-to-end' policy terminology. Training approximately 1 M total pairs, about 300 K oracle+200 K DAgger+25 K collision per R2R / RxR , with general VQA co-training;8 A 100 ×30 h. The 500 K R2R-only model is transferred zero-shot to RxR ; the best 2 history frame version trains both R2R / RxR . Appendix B freezes vision and fine-tunes the projector and Qwen2 for one epoch at 1e-6 using bfloat16; SigLIP features have width 1152 and Qwen2 hidden width 3584. Exact loss masks were not established in the released source audit. At inference maintain ASM, current RGB and optionally 2 history frames, then parse actions. Appendix A explicitly adds 600K general vision-language samples alongside500K navigation samples for the R2R recipe. Its expert-data prose says300K, while Eq 5 says approximately 200K; the total counts therefore have an internal ambiguity. Navigation-pair counts must not be treated as total training exposure.
mapnav.results: Table 1 RGB -only within MapNav 27.1 SR/23.5 SPL →ASM 36.5/34.3 R2R ; adding 2 history frames and RxR training 39.7/37.2 and RxR 32.6/27.7. This supports ASM within backbone; changing training data limits attributing all best model gain to history. Table 4 semantic map 29.1 SR vs ASM 36.5, but prose says original map improves baseline although 26.4<27.3. Table 5 oracle 23.9→ DAgger 33.5→collision 36.5 SR shows substantial data contribution. Table 3 .17 MB constant representation vs NaVid 276 MB at 300 steps is stored observation memory, not full model/ GPU memory; .25 s vs 1.22 s needs whole pipeline accounting. Real 50 instructions five environments show semantic advantages but small samples. Appendix Tables 6–7 isolate input rendering and segmenter choice: directly adding depth reduces SR 27.1→23.1, whereas ASM reaches 36.5. YOLOv8/MobileSAM/Mask2Former yield31.5/34.8/36.5 SR, showing sensitivity to perception quality. This supports the representation interface but does not establish the same mechanism under equally accurate semantic inputs.

progressthink.method:
Section 3 uses two NVILA-2B models: a progress reasoner and an action policy. Let I be an instruction with |I| tokens and O_t the observed history. The reasoner predicts completed instruction text. For each candidate prefix length k∈{1,…,|I|}, Eq.2 defines p(k) proportional to exp(−CE_k/τ), where CE_k compares the predicted text with I's first k tokens and τ>0 is a temperature. The expected prefix length is k̂_t=Σ_k k p(k). The prefix loss is −τ logΣ_k exp(−CE_k/τ). A second loss, max(0,k̂_early−k̂_late), penalizes decreases between ordered observations (Eqs 3–5). The paper does not resolve whether prefix CE is summed or averaged, which affects length bias; no zero-length prefix is listed. A constant estimate satisfies monotonicity, so these constraints alone do not identify true progress.

Stage 2 freezes the progress model and trains the policy on the full instruction, images and predicted progress, using cross-entropy for the next three actions (Eqs 6–7). Stage 3 samples four progress/action alternatives and jointly updates both models with a clipped GRPO objective. The action reward is the number of consecutive correct actions before the first error; the format reward checks syntax. The progress-length reward gives 1 to any text no longer than I and penalizes only excess length (Eqs 8–11). Thus a short but wrong progress statement receives the full length reward. Eq.14 multiplies progress-model and action-model probability ratios, forming a joint importance ratio; zero-variance group handling is not specified in the displayed advantage equation.

Training uses R2R/RxR/ScaleVLN state-action pairs plus 500K DAgger examples; the wording around1.2M examples per dataset is ambiguous. Stages 1–2 run one epoch at 1e-5; stage 3 runs3,000 updates at 1e-6, clipping 0.28 and KL coefficient 0. Eight H20 GPUs are used for roughly 8+60+60 hours. At inference the policy predicts and executes three parameterized actions (25/50/75 cm forward or 15/30/45° turns). Completed-history progress can be monotone, but the robot's current stage can regress after an error; treating the former as sufficient for action is an assumption.

streamvln.method:
SectionIII organizes observations and predicted actions as an interleaved conversation. KV states are reused within an eight-turn window. At a boundary, the model discards the old prompt/action context, samples eight visual memory frames and starts a new window from those features. This lowers repeated prefilling cost while retaining a limited history. The policy predicts four actions per generation; eight turns therefore need not mean eight simulator steps.

An optional geometric variant (Algorithm 1) back-projects image patches using depth and poses into3D voxels. It retains the latest patch token for each stride-bin/voxel pair and can drop frames retaining too few patches. This is deterministic geometric selection, not a learned world model or a guarantee that the remaining patches preserve task-relevant detail. The RGB-only deployed agent must be distinguished from this depth/odometry variant.

The LLaVA-Video-7B/Qwen2 backbone receives two supervised fine-tuning stages: oracle navigation first, then DAgger and general vision-language data. Reported learning rates are2e-5 for language and 5e-6 for vision, with about 1,500 A 100 GPU-hours. The mixture includes450K MP3D navigation examples,300K ScaleVLN examples from 700 HM3D scenes,240K DAgger examples,248K video/ScanQA examples and 230K MMC4 examples. These data additions explain part of the headline gain. At inference, streaming cache reuse controls repeated computation, while window resets and finite memory introduce latency spikes and potential forgetting.

susa.method:
Section 3 augments DUET at two scales. The local semantic branch generates 36 BLIP2-FlanT5-XXL view captions and encodes them with CLIP. Static caption/instruction matching takes maximum word similarities from a 36×L matrix, where L is instruction length. Dynamic cross-attention adds context-dependent matching. The printed Eqs 1–3 are not completely explicit about the projection needed to align vector scores and transformer outputs; the released branch fusion is described separately below.

The global spatial branch uses a Gibson-pretrained ResNet50 depth encoder alongside CLIP RGB features. A shared two-layer panorama transformer and average pooling produce768-dimensional topological node representations; cross-modal and graph attention relate them to the instruction. The four branches are global RGB, global depth, local RGB and local semantic features. Their pooled representations and language feed fusion and symmetric contrastive alignment (Eqs 4–9).

The reported fine-tuning objective is0.2 times expert-action CE plus DAgger-action CE plus 0.8 times symmetric contrastive loss (Eqs 10–11). For an action distribution p_t over candidates, CE is −log p_t(a*_t); the contrastive objective aligns matched visual/language representations while using other batch examples as negatives. The paper reports partial RGB-base pretraining with MLM/MRC/SAP/object-grounding tasks and 100K iterations at batch 32. Fine-tuning uses 25K iterations and task-dependent batches on one RTX4090. Continuous-environment transfer uses an ETPNav planner/executor. Inference fuses branch logits within the DUET policy; the captions are preprocessed representations, not generated step-by-step reasoning.

uninavid.method:
SectionIV encodes each RGB frame with EVA-CLIP into256 patch features. Grid pooling retains 64 tokens for the current frame, four tokens per short-term frame (buffer size 64), and one token for each older frame. When adjacent old tokens have cosine similarity above 0.95, the paper merges them with a count-weighted mean; otherwise it appends a new token (Eqs 1–6). If all frames are sufficiently distinct, the long-term list grows linearly, so merging is not a hard memory bound. The released threshold and empty-cache handling differ from the displayed paper pseudocode, as recorded below.

A two-layer MLP projects visual features into Vicuna-7B. Special navigation markers distinguish action generation from question answering. The action vocabulary is forward 25 cm, left30°, right30° and STOP, with four actions generated per decision. Stage 1 aligns the projector on LLaMA-VID data; stage 2 tunes the projector and language model, keeping vision frozen. The total mixture is5.9M examples:3.6M navigation and 2.3M video QA. Navigation includes2.4M VLN,483K ObjectNav,240K EQA action examples plus 10K answers, and 544K following examples across861 scenes. Training takes about 40 H800 GPUs×35 hours.

For EQA, the agent first navigates, then removes the navigation marker and answers from observed history after STOP. This separates action and answer modes; it does not supply future-state prediction. Real deployment generates four actions in approximately 0.2s on a remote A 100 and uploads new observations asynchronously. Robot heights/radii are varied in training, but the authors explicitly limit claims to the trained range rather than arbitrary embodiments.

INSPECTED CODE. SimplerEnv/simpler_env/policies/openvla/openvla_train.py:49–75 inserts LoRA and exposes the trainable value head;104–109 creates separate AdamW optimizers. Its action evaluation returns scalar values/log probabilities, and 273–319 implements clipped PPO, clipped Huber value loss and entropy regularization, followed by shared gradient clipping and both optimizer steps. The total minimized loss is policy_loss + value_loss − entropy_coefficient × entropy; accumulation divides this loss before backward.

In the a 0 path at 690–716, the pre-action hidden state gives a B×1 value, action logits have shape B×7×256, and seven token log probabilities are summed to form the joint action log probability. This matches Appendix A.1's product-of-token-probabilities convention. The fetched eval_ms3_collect.py:23–44,62–78,90–128 is an Octo data-collection utility, not an RL4VLA performance evaluator; it is explicitly not treated as validation of the paper's PPO evaluation. Full main training orchestration, all reward/task implementations and the exact final evaluator remain outside this targeted source audit. No project code was executed.
rl4vla.method:
Section 3 uses OpenVLA: SigLIP and DINOv2 image features feed Llama2-7B, which predicts a seven-dimensional end-effector/gripper action. Each action coordinate is discretized into256 bins between training quantiles. The base setting observes one 640×480 image and an instruction. All compared fine-tuning methods use rank 32 LoRA; the value head is fully trained.

Appendix A.1, Eqs 1–2 defines PPO with scalar ratio r_t=πθ(a_t|s_t)/πold(a_t|s_t), where π(a_t|s_t) is the product of the seven action-token probabilities. The maximized surrogate is E[min(r_t A_t, clip(r_t,1−ε,1+ε)A_t)]. GAE estimates A_t by summing discounted temporal-difference residuals, Σ_l(γλ)^l[r_(t+l)+γV(s_(t+l+1))−V(s_(t+l))]. These are policy-gradient estimators, not a convergence guarantee. The three-layer shared critic reads the first action-token hidden state. GRPO instead uses 32 groups of 8 trajectories and group-normalized terminal outcomes; TPO/DPO compares whole trajectory preferences using the same sparse reward.

The base pick-and-place reward gives partial credit for grasping/holding and a larger terminal placement reward. A 140-demonstration warm start reduces interaction requirements. Motion-planner demonstrations are filtered when translation is below 0.01 and Euler-angle change below 0.06 (Appendix A.2), removing about one third of idle actions. This preprocessing is important when comparing SFT and RL. The shared critic uses 44.4 GB versus 81.3 GB for a separate critic; the main run takes roughly 42 hours on one A 100. Appendix B.5 adds four-action chunks with action-dimension clipping and retuned γ/λ, so it is a separate recipe. Appendix B.6 adds articulated-object opening on a Franka robot, extending the original pick-and-place scope.
rl4vla.results:
Figure 3 compares PPO, GRPO and DPO under the authors' setup; it supports PPO as a strong baseline, not a universal ordering of optimizers. Appendix Table 1 reports task success: in-distribution SFT0.781 versus RL0.938; unseen objects0.453 versus 0.714; changed robot pose0.339 versus 0.797; mid-episode object repositioning0.286 versus 0.745. Because base success differs, relative degradation as well as absolute SR matters. Figure 7 reports similar relative visual robustness and stronger semantic/execution transfer.

The extended tests qualify the conclusion. With action chunks, Table 3 shows a regression on unseen multiple receptacles (0.365 SFT versus 0.297 RL). On articulated objects, Table 4 reports visual-average SR 0.646 versus 0.591 and rephrased-instruction SR 0.703 versus 0.620; RL improves execution-average SR 0.300→0.398. Thus RL does not uniformly improve every semantic or visual shift. Thirty preliminary real trials in Table 2 yield pick-and-place SR 0 versus 0.27, which is promising but small. These manipulation findings motivate matched tests in VLN; they are not navigation results.

Appendix A.2 supplies a practical fallback omitted from the core expectation equation: if the minimum sampling probability exceeds the budget at extremely long horizons, remove the oldest frames. Consequently the unresolved issue is evidence loss under truncation and whether every stochastic draw respects the intended budget, rather than an assertion that the entire method has no fallback.
